title: Yeet, Fermented Dried Sea Snail
author: Compiled from Morinière (CRODT) and Essuman (FAO Fisheries Technical Paper 329)
desc: Cymbium whelk flesh removed from the shell, split in four, buried in sand or under old nets for a day (FAO: 2 to 4 days), washed and sun-dried two days until the whole treatment has taken 64% of the weight off — a semi-dry light brown product with a strong smell.
longDesc: Yeet, the ‘Senegalese camembert’, is a fermented, dried sea-snail seasoning used in ceebu jën and soupou kandia. The shell and viscera are removed and the foot split in four lengthwise. At the landing site the pieces are placed in sand or under used nets for 24 hours to ferment, cleaned, and sun-dried for two days; the whole treatment results in a weight loss of 64% — the one measurable endpoint anywhere in the literature. FAO describes the finished product as a semi-dry light brown product with a strong smell, which redried becomes hard and dark brown. FAO gives longer times (2 to 4 days of fermentation in tanks, jute bags or polysacks, then 2 to 4 days of drying on raised platforms) — the two sources disagree and are not reconciled. No salt is mentioned in either. No pH, salt level, water activity or microbiology has ever been published for yeet.
ingredients: Sand or used nets for the ferment (CRODT), or fermentation tanks, jute bags or polysacks (FAO)
steps: Remove the shell and the viscera. Split the foot in four lengthwise (FAO: into two or four parts).
Place the pieces in sand, or under used nets, for 24 hours (CRODT), or in tanks, jute bags or polysacks for 2 to 4 days (FAO). No salting is mentioned.
Clean the pieces (a non-peer-reviewed source adds washing in four to five waters) and dry them in the sun for 2 days (CRODT) or on raised platforms for 2 to 4 days (FAO).

Weigh in and weigh out: the whole treatment takes the pieces down by 64% of their starting weight (CRODT). The finished yeet is semi-dry, light brown, with a strong smell; re-drying makes it hard and dark brown.
Rinse before use; a non-peer-reviewed source blanches it 5 minutes in boiling water to firm it.
chefTips: The one hard number is the 64% weight loss across fermentation and drying.
Finished: ‘a semi-dry light brown product with a strong smell’ (FAO 329).
It is susceptible to a lot of mould growth and keeps about two months (FAO).
commonMistakes: Judging by days alone: the two published fermentation times differ by up to four-fold.
Trusting a home ferment: no safety limits have been established for yeet.
Re-drying hard — FAO notes redrying makes it hard and dark brown.
healthBenefits: A protein-dense seasoning; no nutrition or safety data has been published for yeet.
culturalNote: CRODT’s Morinière records that the two operations give yeet ‘son goût particulier’ and its nickname ‘camembert sénégalais’, and make it a condiment of choice for perfuming dishes; the work is done by fishermen’s wives at the landing site. A further source (ICSF/CREDETIP, 2002) says traditional yeet is buried in the ground 3 to 4 days and that its drying was extended from three days to almost a month for Asian buyers who wanted a hygienic, reddish product — conflicting with the 24-hour and 2-day figures.
sources: Morinière, P., ‘Biologie et pêche de Cymbium pepo (Lightfoot, 1786) au Sénégal’, CRODT document scientifique (series number OCR-garbled, probably 77; year not legible, fishery data March 1979 – April 1980). TWO-PASS, French fragments: ‘placés dans le sable ou sous les filets usagés pendant 24 h afin de fermenter’; ‘séchage … pendant deux jours’; ‘perte de poids de 64 %’; nickname ‘camembert sénégalais’. Verify the series number and year against a library record before citing.

Essuman, K.M. (1992), FAO Fisheries Technical Paper 329 (TWO-PASS): ‘Yeet is a semi-dry light brown product with a strong smell.’; ‘Redrying results in a hard product which is dark brown in colour.’; fermentation two to four days; drying two to four days.

CONFLICT recorded, unreconciled: CRODT 24 h vs FAO 2–4 days; ICSF buried in the ground 3–4 days. Fermenting Cultures (Ferment #16; no byline, no date) adds sand burial for ‘several days’, washing in four to five waters and blanching 5 minutes to firm — treated as non-peer-reviewed.
No pH, salt figure, water activity or microbiology exists for yeet in anything reached. Times above use the CRODT figures (24 h plus 2 days).
